_meta.note: General practice problems written for InterviewPilot AI. They are not questions from any company. Generated by scripts/build_coding_problems.py

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.statement:
Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices `[i, j]` of the two numbers that add up to `target`, with `i < j`.

Exactly one such pair exists. You may not use the same element twice.
constraints: Return the indices in increasing order: [i, j] with i < j

examples.explanation: `nums[0] + nums[1] = 2 + 7 = 9`, so the answer is `[0, 1]`.

problems.approach: Scan once, remembering each value's index in a dictionary. For each number, check whether its complement (target minus the number) was already seen. This is O(n) instead of the O(n^2) pair-by-pair search.

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.statement:
Given a string `s` containing only the characters `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}`, return `True` if the brackets are valid and `False` otherwise.

A string is valid when every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, in the correct order. The empty string is valid.

examples.explanation: `()[]{}` is valid: every bracket is closed in order.
`(]` is not valid: `]` does not match `(`.

problems.approach: Push each opening bracket on a stack. For a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener (and the stack must not be empty). At the end the stack must be empty.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.statement:
Given a list of lowercase words, group the words that are anagrams of each other and return the groups as a list of lists.

Ordering is fixed so the answer is unique: inside a group, keep the words in their original order; order the groups by where their first word appears in the input. Duplicate words are kept.
constraints: Each word has 0 to 20 lowercase letters a-z
Two words are anagrams when they contain the same letters the same number of times

examples.explanation: `eat`, `tea`, `ate` are anagrams, so they form the first group in input order.

problems.approach: Use the sorted letters of each word as a dictionary key; words with the same key are anagrams. A dict keeps first-seen order, which gives the required group order.

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.statement:
Given a list of intervals `[start, end]` (with `start <= end`), merge all overlapping intervals and return the result sorted by `start`.

Two intervals overlap when they share at least one point, so `[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]` merge into `[1, 5]`. The input may be unsorted.
constraints: Return a new list sorted by start; merged intervals do not overlap or touch

examples.explanation: `[1, 3]` and `[2, 6]` overlap, so they merge into `[1, 6]`.
`[1, 4]` and `[4, 5]` touch at 4, so they merge into `[1, 5]`.

problems.approach: Sort by start. Walk through the intervals keeping the last merged one; if the next start is within the last end, extend it, otherwise start a new merged interval.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.statement:
Given a list of integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent values.

Order the result by frequency (highest first). When two values have the same frequency, the smaller value comes first.
constraints: 1 <= k <= number of distinct values in nums

examples.explanation: `1` appears 3 times and `2` appears 2 times, so `[1, 2]`.
`4` and `5` both appear twice; the smaller value `4` comes first.

problems.approach: Count occurrences, then sort the distinct values by (-count, value) and take the first k. A heap gives O(n log k).
problems.reference_solution:
def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    from collections import Counter
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return sorted(counts, key=lambda v: (-counts[v], v))[:k]

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.statement:
Given a list `nums` sorted in ascending order with no duplicates, and an integer `target`, return the index of `target` in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not present.

Your solution should run in O(log n) time. (The automatic tests check correctness; the expected complexity is explained after you finish.)
constraints: nums is sorted ascending and contains distinct integers

examples.explanation: `9` is at index 4.
`2` is not in the list, so the answer is `-1`.

problems.approach: Keep a window [lo, hi]. Compare the middle element with the target and discard the half that cannot contain it. Be careful with the loop condition so the last remaining element is checked.

problems.title: Word Frequency
problems.statement:
Given a string `text`, count how often each word appears and return a list of `[word, count]` pairs.

A word is a maximal run of ASCII letters (a-z, A-Z). Everything else (digits, spaces, punctuation, apostrophes) separates words. Words are compared in lowercase. Sort the pairs by count (highest first), then by word alphabetically.
constraints: Only ASCII letters form words, so `it's` is the two words `it` and `s`
Return an empty list when there are no words

examples.explanation: `the` appears twice; the other words once each, in alphabetical order.
All three spellings are the same word `hello`.

args: The quick brown fox. The lazy dog! the end?

problems.approach: Extract words with a regular expression, lowercase them, count with a Counter, then sort by (-count, word).
problems.reference_solution:
def word_frequency(text):
    import re
    from collections import Counter
    counts = Counter(w.lower() for w in re.findall(r'[A-Za-z]+', text))
    return [[w, c] for w, c in sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))]

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.statement:
Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character.

A substring is a contiguous part of the string.
constraints: s may contain any printable ASCII characters, including spaces

examples.explanation: `abc` is the longest run without repeats, so the answer is `3`.
`wke` has length 3; `pwke` is not contiguous.

problems.approach: Slide a window. Remember the last index of every character; when a character repeats inside the window, move the window start just past its previous position.

problems.title: Precision, Recall and F1
problems.statement:
Given two equal-length lists of 0/1 labels, `y_true` (the real labels) and `y_pred` (the predictions), compute precision, recall and F1 for the positive class `1`. Return `[precision, recall, f1]`, each rounded to 4 decimal places with Python's `round()`.

precision = TP / (TP + FP), recall = TP / (TP + FN), f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall). If a denominator is 0, that value is `0.0` (so f1 is `0.0` when precision + recall is 0).
constraints: TP = predicted 1 and truly 1; FP = predicted 1 but truly 0; FN = predicted 0 but truly 1

examples.explanation: TP=2, FP=1, FN=1, so precision, recall and F1 are all 2/3 = 0.6667.
With no positives at all, every value is `0.0`.

problems.approach: Count true positives, false positives and false negatives in one pass, then apply the formulas, guarding every division against a zero denominator.
problems.reference_solution:
def classification_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    tp = sum(1 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred) if t == 1 and p == 1)
    fp = sum(1 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred) if t == 0 and p == 1)
    fn = sum(1 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred) if t == 1 and p == 0)
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return [round(precision, 4), round(recall, 4), round(f1, 4)]

problems.title: Min-Max Scaling
problems.statement:
Scale a list of numbers to the range 0 to 1 with min-max scaling: `(x - min) / (max - min)`. Return a new list with each value rounded to 6 decimal places using Python's `round()`.

If all values are equal (so `max == min`), return `0.0` for every value. An empty list gives an empty list.
constraints: Return floats, in the original order

examples.explanation: Min is 1 and max is 3, so the values become `[0.0, 0.5, 1.0]`.
All values are equal, so every output is `0.0`.

problems.approach: Find the minimum and maximum once, handle the all-equal and empty cases first, then apply the formula to every value.

problems.title: Remove Duplicates, Keep Order
problems.statement:
Given a list `items` of integers, return a new list that contains each value only once, keeping the order of its FIRST appearance.

Example idea: a set remembers what you have already seen while a loop builds the answer.
constraints: Return a new list; do not sort

examples.explanation: `3` and `1` repeat, so only their first appearance is kept: `[3, 1, 2]`.
All values are `5`, so one `5` remains.

problems.approach: Loop once. A set gives O(1) 'have I seen this?' checks; append to the result only when the value is new.

problems.title: Common Elements of Two Lists
problems.statement: Given two lists of integers `a` and `b`, return a sorted list of the values that appear in BOTH lists. Each common value appears once in the answer, even if it repeats in the inputs.
constraints: Return the values in ascending order

examples.explanation: `2` and `3` are in both lists, so `[2, 3]`.
Nothing is shared, so the answer is `[]`.

problems.approach: Turn both lists into sets and intersect them; sort the result.
problems.reference_solution:
def common_elements(a, b):
    return sorted(set(a) & set(b))

problems.title: Student Grade Report
problems.statement:
`marks` is a dictionary that maps a student name to a list of that student's marks (0 to 100). For each student compute the average (rounded to 2 decimals with `round()`) and a grade: `A` for average >= 85, `B` for >= 70, `C` for >= 50, otherwise `F`. A student with an empty list has average `0.0` and grade `F`.

Return a list of `[name, average, grade]`, sorted by average (highest first), then by name alphabetically.

examples.explanation: Ali averages 85.0 (grade `A`); Sara averages 65.0 (`C`).
An empty list gives `0.0` and `F`.

problems.approach: Loop over the dictionary items, compute the average, choose the grade with if / elif, then sort with a (-average, name) key.

problems.title: Invoice Total with Discount and Tax
problems.statement:
`items` is a list of `[name, unit_price, quantity]`. Compute the subtotal (sum of price * quantity). Apply a discount to the subtotal: 15% if the subtotal is more than 10000, otherwise 10% if it is more than 5000, otherwise none. Then add 17% sales tax on the discounted amount.

Return `[subtotal, discount_amount, tax_amount, total]`, each rounded to 2 decimals with `round()`.

examples.explanation: Subtotal 1100, no discount, tax 187, total 1287.
Subtotal 6000 gets a 10% discount (600), tax is 17% of 5400.

problems.approach: Sum price * quantity in one loop, pick the discount rate with if / elif / else (note the boundaries: exactly 5000 or 10000 gets the lower rate), then apply tax to the discounted amount.

problems.title: Suspicious Failed Logins
problems.statement:
`events` is a list of `[user, result]` in time order, where `result` is `"ok"` or `"fail"`. A user is suspicious if they have 3 or more `"fail"` events IN A ROW (a successful login resets that user's streak; other users' events do not).

Return the sorted list of suspicious users, each once.

examples.explanation: `ali` fails three times in a row, so `["ali"]`.
`sara`'s streak is reset by `ok`, so nobody is flagged.

problems.approach: Keep a dict of current failure streaks per user. A failure increases the streak (flag the user at 3); a success resets it to 0. A set avoids duplicates.

problems.title: Bank Ledger
problems.statement:
`transactions` is a list of `[account, kind, amount]` where `kind` is `"deposit"` or `"withdraw"`. Every account starts at balance 0. Process the transactions in order:
- a deposit adds `amount`;
- a withdraw subtracts `amount` ONLY if the balance is enough; otherwise the transaction is rejected and the balance does not change.

Return `[balances, rejected]`, where `balances` is a dictionary account -> final balance (every account that appears is included) and `rejected` is the list of indexes (0-based) of rejected transactions.
constraints: An account that only has rejected withdrawals still appears with balance 0

examples.explanation: A ends with 70; B never had money, so its withdrawal (index 2) is rejected.
Withdrawing exactly the balance is allowed.

problems.approach: Walk through the list once with enumerate, keeping balances in a dict. Check the balance before a withdraw and record the index when it is rejected.

problems.title: Custom FizzBuzz
problems.statement:
`rules` is a list of `[divisor, word]` pairs in priority order. For every number `i` from 1 to `n` (inclusive) build a string by appending `word` for each rule whose divisor divides `i` (in the order of the rules). If no rule matches, use `str(i)`.

Return the list of `n` strings. Classic FizzBuzz is `rules = [[3, "Fizz"], [5, "Buzz"]]`.

examples.explanation: `["1", "2", "Fizz", "4", "Buzz"]` for n=5 with the classic rules.
With no rules every number stays as text.

problems.approach: Nested loops: for each number check every rule with the modulo operator and join the matching words; fall back to the number.

problems.title: Find the Missing Numbers
problems.statement: `nums` contains distinct integers that were taken from the range `1..n`. Return the sorted list of the numbers from `1` to `n` that are NOT in `nums`.
constraints: Every value of nums is between 1 and n and appears once

examples.explanation: `3` and `5` are missing from `1..5`, so `[3, 5]`.
Nothing is present, so all numbers are missing.

problems.approach: Put nums in a set for fast lookups, then loop through 1..n and keep the numbers that are absent.

problems.title: Unique Pairs with a Given Sum
problems.statement: Given a list `nums` and an integer `target`, return all UNIQUE pairs `[a, b]` with `a <= b` and `a + b == target`, sorted ascending. Two pairs are the same if they contain the same two values. A value may be used twice only if it appears at least twice in `nums`.
constraints: Return a sorted list of `[a, b]` lists

examples.explanation: `2` appears three times, so `[2, 2]` is valid once.

problems.approach: One pass with a set of seen values: if the complement was already seen, record the pair as a sorted tuple in another set (which removes duplicates), then sort the tuples.

problems.title: Server Log Summary
problems.statement:
Each log line looks like `"LEVEL: message"`. Count how many lines have each level among `INFO`, `WARN` and `ERROR` (the level is the text before the FIRST colon, compared exactly). Lines with any other level, or without a colon, are ignored.

Return a dictionary with the keys `INFO`, `WARN` and `ERROR` (always all three, count 0 when absent).
constraints: The message may itself contain colons

examples.explanation: Two `INFO` lines and one `ERROR` line.
`DEBUG` and the line without a colon are ignored.

problems.approach: Start with a dict of zero counts, split each line once at the first colon (`split(':', 1)`) and count only the known levels.

problems.title: Flatten a Nested List
problems.statement: `data` is a list that may contain integers and other lists (nested to any depth). Return one flat list with all the integers in their original left-to-right order.

examples.explanation: Empty lists vanish.

problems.approach: Use recursion or an explicit stack of iterators: when an element is a list, go into it, otherwise append the number.

problems.title: Password Rule Checker
problems.statement:
Check a password against these rules and return the list of FAILED rule names, in exactly this order:
1. `length`: at least 8 characters
2. `lower`: has a lowercase letter
3. `upper`: has an uppercase letter
4. `digit`: has a digit
5. `special`: has a character that is not a letter or digit
6. `space`: contains NO space (fails if it has one)

A valid password returns an empty list.
constraints: Use plain ASCII logic: letters a-z/A-Z and digits 0-9

examples.explanation: `Passw0rd!` passes every rule: `[]`.
`abc` is short and has no uppercase letter, digit or special character.

problems.approach: Check each rule with a small condition or `any(...)` over the characters and append the rule name when it fails, keeping the required order.

problems.title: Merge User Records
problems.statement:
`primary` and `updates` are lists of user dictionaries; each has an `"id"` and any other fields. Build one record per id: start from the record in `primary` and apply every update for that id in order (later values replace earlier values; new keys are added). Ids that only appear in `updates` are included too.

Return the merged records as a list sorted by `id`.
constraints: `id` is an integer; ids are unique inside `primary`
`updates` may contain the same id several times

examples.explanation: Ali's record gets the new `city` key.
An update for an unknown id creates a new record.

problems.approach: Index the primary records by id in a dict, apply updates with `dict.update`, then sort the keys to produce the final list.

problems.title: Rate Limiter
problems.statement:
An API allows at most `limit` accepted requests in any window of `window` seconds. `times` is the sorted list of request timestamps (integers, seconds). A request at time `t` is accepted only if fewer than `limit` ACCEPTED requests happened at times `> t - window` (so the window is `(t - window, t]`). Rejected requests do not count.

Return a list of booleans, `True` for accepted and `False` for rejected, one per request.

examples.explanation: The first two requests fit; the next two are rejected within 10 seconds.
With limit 1 and window 5, a request exactly 5 seconds later is accepted.

problems.approach: Keep a queue of accepted timestamps. Drop the ones that left the window, accept when the queue is shorter than the limit.

problems.title: Department Salary Stats
problems.statement:
`employees` is a list of `[name, department, salary]`. For every department return `[department, headcount, average_salary, top_earner]` where the average is rounded to 2 decimals with `round()` and the top earner is the employee with the highest salary (if tied, the alphabetically smaller name).

Return the rows sorted by department name.

examples.explanation: IT has 2 people, average 150.0, top earner `Sara`.
A tie on salary picks the alphabetically smaller name.

problems.approach: Group rows into a dict of lists by department, then for each department (sorted) compute count, mean and the top earner with a (-salary, name) key.

problems.title: Clean Messy Records
constraints: The first occurrence of a duplicate pair is the one kept

examples.explanation: The first row becomes `["Ali Khan", 25, "Lahore"]`; the others are invalid.
The second row repeats the same name and city, so it is dropped.

problems.approach: Loop over the rows, strip and validate with conditions, convert the age, and use a set of lowercase (name, city) tuples to skip duplicates.

problems.title: Game Leaderboard
problems.statement: `scores` is a list of `[player, points]` events (a player can appear many times; points add up). Return the leaderboard as a list of `[rank, player, total]`, sorted by total points (highest first) and then by player name. Players with the same total share the same rank (ranks are `1, 2, 2, 3...`, with no gaps after a tie).

examples.explanation: `a` totals 25 and `b` totals 20, so `a` is rank 1.
`x` and `y` tie at rank 1; `z` is rank 2 (dense ranking).

problems.approach: Sum the points per player in a dict, sort by (-total, name) and assign dense ranks that only increase when the total changes.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Run
problems.statement: Given an unsorted list of integers `nums`, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (like `4, 5, 6, 7`) that can be formed from its values. Duplicates are ignored. Aim for O(n) using a set instead of sorting.

examples.explanation: `1, 2, 3, 4` is the longest run, so the answer is 4.
Duplicates of `1` count once.

problems.approach: Put all numbers in a set. Only start counting from numbers whose predecessor is missing (run starts); extend while the next number exists.

problems.title: Minimum Meeting Rooms
problems.statement: `meetings` is a list of `[start, end]` times (with `start < end`). Two meetings overlap if one starts BEFORE the other ends; a meeting that starts exactly when another ends can use the same room. Return the minimum number of rooms needed to hold all meetings.

examples.explanation: The first meeting overlaps both others, so 2 rooms are needed.
Back-to-back meetings can share a room.

problems.approach: Sort start times and end times separately and sweep: a new meeting needs a room unless an earlier meeting has already ended.
problems.reference_solution:
def min_rooms(meetings):
    starts = sorted(m[0] for m in meetings)
    ends = sorted(m[1] for m in meetings)
    rooms = best = j = 0
    for s in starts:
        while ends[j] <= s:
            j += 1
            rooms -= 1
        rooms += 1
        best = max(best, rooms)
    return best

problems.title: Inventory Restock
problems.statement:
`stock` is a dictionary item -> quantity in stock, and `minimum` is a dictionary item -> minimum quantity that must be kept. For every item in `minimum` that is below its minimum (an item missing from `stock` counts as 0), the shop must order the difference.

Return a list of `[item, quantity_to_order]` sorted by item name. Items that already have enough stock are left out.
constraints: Items in `stock` that are not in `minimum` are ignored

examples.explanation: Only `pen` is below its minimum, by 2.
A missing item counts as 0 in stock.

problems.approach: Loop over the sorted minimum dictionary, read the stock with `dict.get(item, 0)` and add the shortfall when stock is lower.

problems.title: Primes up to N
problems.statement: Return the list of all prime numbers less than or equal to `n`, in ascending order. A prime is a number greater than 1 with no divisors other than 1 and itself. The sieve of Eratosthenes keeps this fast for large `n`.
constraints: n = 0 or 1 gives an empty list

examples.explanation: `2, 3, 5, 7` are the primes up to 10.
There are no primes up to 1.

problems.approach: Make a list of booleans; for each prime i mark its multiples from i*i as not prime. The numbers still marked True are the primes.

problems.title: Run-Length Encoding
problems.statement:
Compress a string by replacing each run of the same character with the character followed by the run length, but write nothing for a run of length 1. Example: `"aaabccdd"` becomes `"a3bc2d2"`.

Return the compressed string. A run of length 1 stays as the single character.
constraints: The empty string gives the empty string

examples.explanation: No repeats means the string is unchanged.

problems.approach: Walk with two indexes: find the end of the current run, append the character and the count (only when the count is above 1).

problems.title: Roman Numeral to Integer
problems.statement: Convert a Roman numeral to an integer. Symbols: `I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000`. When a smaller symbol comes BEFORE a larger one it is subtracted (`IV = 4`, `IX = 9`, `XL = 40`, `XC = 90`, `CD = 400`, `CM = 900`), otherwise it is added. The input is always a valid numeral from 1 to 3999.
constraints: Input uses only the seven uppercase symbols
problems.approach: Use a dict of symbol values. Look one symbol ahead: if the next symbol is larger, subtract the current value, otherwise add it.

problems.title: Filter Palindromes
problems.statement: From a list of phrases, return the phrases that are palindromes when you ignore case and ignore everything that is not a letter or digit (letters a-z, A-Z, digits 0-9). An empty cleaned phrase does NOT count. Keep the original phrase text and the original order, and keep a phrase only the first time it appears (exact same text).
constraints: Each phrase has at most 200 characters
Compare phrases for duplicates exactly as written

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
output: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
examples.explanation: `Racecar` and the Panama phrase read the same both ways.
Punctuation-only text is ignored and does not count.

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
expected: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

problems.approach: Clean each phrase into a list of lowercase alphanumeric characters, compare with its reverse, and use a set to drop repeated phrases.

problems.title: Moving Average
problems.statement: Given a list of numbers `values` and a window size `k`, return the list of averages of every `k` consecutive values, each rounded to 2 decimals with `round()`. The answer has `len(values) - k + 1` numbers. If `k` is larger than the list, return an empty list.

examples.explanation: A window larger than the list gives `[]`.

problems.approach: Keep a running window sum: add the new value and remove the one that left. This is O(n) instead of re-adding k values each time.

problems.title: Shopping Cart by Category
problems.statement:
`cart` is a list of `[product, category, price, quantity]`. Group by category and return a list of `[category, total, products]` where `total` is the sum of price * quantity (an integer; prices are whole numbers) and `products` is the sorted list of DISTINCT product names in that category.

Sort the result by total (highest first), then by category name.
constraints: The same product can appear on several lines

examples.explanation: `elec` totals 400 and `food` totals 100; `elec` comes first.
Duplicate product names appear once in the list but both lines count in the total.

problems.approach: Use one dict for totals and one dict of sets for distinct products, then sort the rows by (-total, category).

problems.title: Spiral Order of a Matrix
problems.statement: Given a rectangular matrix (list of equal-length rows), return all its elements in spiral order: left to right along the top row, down the right column, right to left along the bottom row, up the left column, then continue inward.
constraints: All rows have the same length

examples.explanation: A single row is read left to right.

problems.approach: Track four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and walk the edges, shrinking the boundaries after each lap. Guard the last two edges so a single remaining row or column is not read twice.

problems.title: First Non-Repeating Character
problems.statement: Return the INDEX of the first character in `s` that appears exactly once in the whole string, or `-1` if there is none.
constraints: s may contain any printable ASCII characters

examples.explanation: `l` appears once and is at index 0.
Every character repeats, so the answer is `-1`.

problems.approach: Count every character with a dict, then scan the string again and return the first index whose count is 1.

problems.title: Reverse the Words
problems.statement: Return the words of `s` in reverse order, joined by a single space. Words are separated by one or more spaces, and the result has no leading or trailing spaces.
constraints: s contains letters, digits and spaces

examples.explanation: `"the sky  is blue"` becomes `"blue is sky the"`.
An empty string stays empty.

problems.approach: Split on whitespace (which drops empty pieces), reverse the list of words and join with one space.
problems.reference_solution:
def reverse_words(s):
    return ' '.join(s.split()[::-1])

problems.title: Digital Root
problems.statement: Repeatedly replace a non-negative integer `n` by the sum of its digits until only one digit is left, and return that digit. Example: `38 -> 3 + 8 = 11 -> 1 + 1 = 2`.

examples.explanation: `38` becomes `11`, then `2`.
A single digit is its own root.

problems.approach: Loop while the number has two or more digits and replace it by its digit sum. (A formula with n % 9 also works, but check the multiples of 9 and zero.)

problems.title: Caesar Cipher
problems.statement: Shift every English letter of `text` forward by `k` places in the alphabet, wrapping around from `z` to `a`. Keep the case of each letter and leave every other character unchanged. `k` may be negative or larger than 26.
constraints: Only the letters a-z and A-Z change

examples.explanation: `x`, `y`, `z` wrap to `a`, `b`, `c`.
Punctuation and digits stay as they are.

problems.approach: Map each letter to 0 to 25, add k, take the result modulo 26 (Python handles negatives correctly) and map back, keeping the original case.

problems.title: Move Zeros to the End
problems.statement: Return a new list in which all zeros of `nums` are moved to the end while the other numbers keep their original order.

examples.explanation: A list of zeros stays as it is.

problems.approach: Keep the non-zero values in order, then append as many zeros as were removed. A two-pointer version does it in place.

problems.title: Stack with Minimum
problems.statement: Simulate a stack that can report its minimum in O(1). `ops` is a list of operations: `["push", x]`, `["pop"]`, `["top"]`, `["min"]`. `pop` on an empty stack does nothing. For every `top` and `min` operation, add its result to the answer, or `None` when the stack is empty. Return the list of these results.
constraints: Each operation must take O(1) time

examples.explanation: After pushing 3 and 1 the minimum is 1; after a pop it is 3.
On an empty stack `top` and `min` give `None`.

problems.approach: Store with every pushed value the minimum of the stack at that moment, so after a pop the previous minimum is already known.

problems.title: Cycle in a Linked List
problems.statement: A linked list is stored in an array: node `i` points to node `nxt[i]`, and `-1` means the end of the list. Starting at node `head` (`-1` for an empty list), return `True` if following the pointers ever visits a node twice, otherwise `False`. Nodes that cannot be reached from `head` do not matter.
constraints: head is -1 or a valid index
Use O(1) extra memory if you can (Floyd's slow and fast pointers)

examples.explanation: `0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1` repeats node 1, so the answer is `True`.
The second list ends at node 2, so `False`.

problems.approach: Move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps. If the list has a cycle they meet; if the fast pointer reaches the end there is none.

problems.title: Level Order of a Tree
problems.statement:
A tree is given as nested lists: a node is `[value, left, right]` and a missing child (or an empty tree) is `None`.

Return the values of the tree level by level, from the top, and from left to right inside each level, as a list of lists. An empty tree gives `[]`.

examples.explanation: The root is level 0, then 9 and 20, then 15 and 7.
A single node gives `[[1]]`.

problems.approach: Process one whole level at a time with a list (or queue): record the level's values, then collect the children for the next level.

problems.title: Valid Binary Search Tree
problems.statement:
A tree is given as nested lists: a node is `[value, left, right]` and a missing child (or an empty tree) is `None`.

Return `True` if the tree is a valid binary search tree: for every node, ALL values in its left subtree are smaller and ALL values in its right subtree are larger (equal values are not allowed). An empty tree is valid.

examples.explanation: The first tree is valid: 1 < 2 < 3.
In the second tree the node 3 sits in the right subtree of 5 but is smaller than 5.

problems.approach: Carry the allowed range (lower and upper bound) down the tree. A node must be strictly inside its range, then its children get narrower ranges.

problems.title: Root-to-Leaf Path Sum
problems.statement:
A tree is given as nested lists: a node is `[value, left, right]` and a missing child (or an empty tree) is `None`.

Return `True` if there is a path from the root down to a LEAF (a node with no children) whose values add up to `target`. An empty tree has no path. Values can be negative.

examples.explanation: The path 5 -> 4 -> 11 -> 2 adds up to 22.
Sums that stop at a node that is not a leaf do not count.

problems.approach: Walk down while keeping the running sum. Only compare with the target when the node is a leaf.

problems.title: Product of the Others
problems.statement: Return a list `out` where `out[i]` is the product of all numbers of `nums` except `nums[i]`. Do it WITHOUT division, because `nums` may contain zeros.
constraints: The answers fit in a normal Python integer

examples.explanation: With one zero, only the position of the zero is non-zero.

problems.approach: Multiply by the product of everything to the left in one pass, then by the product of everything to the right in a second pass.
problems.reference_solution:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

problems.title: Three Numbers that Sum to Zero
problems.statement: Return all UNIQUE triplets `[a, b, c]` of values from `nums` (three different positions) with `a + b + c == 0`. Each triplet is sorted ascending and the list of triplets is sorted too. The same triplet of values must not appear twice.

examples.explanation: `[-1, -1, 2]` and `[-1, 0, 1]` are the two unique triplets.
No three numbers add up to zero in `[0, 1, 1]`.

problems.approach: Sort, fix the first number, then move two pointers inward from both ends. Skip equal values to avoid repeated triplets.

problems.title: Days Until Warmer
problems.statement: `temps[i]` is the temperature on day `i`. Return a list where entry `i` is the number of days you must wait after day `i` for a STRICTLY warmer temperature, or `0` if that never happens.
constraints: A solution that scans forward from every day is too slow

examples.explanation: After 73 the next warmer day is the next one, so `1`.
A temperature that is never exceeded gets `0`.

problems.approach: Keep a stack of days that are still waiting for a warmer day. When a warmer day arrives, pop every colder day and fill in the waiting time.

problems.title: Subarrays with Sum K
problems.statement: Count the continuous, non-empty subarrays of `nums` whose sum equals `k`. The numbers can be negative or zero.

examples.explanation: `[1, 1]` appears twice in `[1, 1, 1]`.
Both `[1, 2]` and `[3]` add up to 3.

problems.approach: Keep a dictionary of how many times each prefix sum was seen. A subarray ending here sums to k for every earlier prefix equal to (current prefix - k).

problems.title: Container with Most Water
problems.statement: `heights[i]` is the height of a vertical line at position `i`. Choose two lines; together with the x-axis they form a container whose water level is the shorter line. Return the largest area, which is (distance between the lines) times (the shorter height).

examples.explanation: Lines 1 and 8 (heights 8 and 7) are 7 apart: 7 x 7 = 49.
Two lines of height 1 that are 1 apart give 1.

problems.approach: Start with the widest container and move the pointer at the shorter line inward, because only a taller line can improve the area.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor
problems.statement:
A tree is given as nested lists: a node is `[value, left, right]` and a missing child (or an empty tree) is `None`.

All values are unique and both `p` and `q` exist in the tree. Return the value of the lowest common ancestor of the nodes with values `p` and `q`: the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree (a node counts as its own descendant). This is a general binary tree, NOT necessarily ordered.

examples.explanation: Nodes 5 and 1 only meet at the root 3.
Node 5 is an ancestor of node 4, so the answer is 5.

problems.approach: Record each node's parent, collect all ancestors of p, then walk up from q until you hit one of them.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.statement: `heights[i]` is the height of a bar of width 1. After rain, water collects between the bars. Return the total units of trapped water.

examples.explanation: Between the bars of height 2 and 3 in the first example, water fills the gaps: 6 units in total.
A rising or falling staircase holds nothing.

problems.approach: Water above a bar is limited by the lower of the highest bars on its left and right. Two pointers track both maxima while moving inward from the lower side.

problems.title: Fewest Coins
problems.statement: Given the coin values `coins` (unlimited supply of each) and an `amount`, return the smallest number of coins that add up to exactly `amount`, or `-1` if it is impossible. An amount of 0 needs 0 coins.
constraints: A greedy choice of the biggest coin is not always correct

examples.explanation: `11 = 5 + 5 + 1` needs 3 coins.
3 cannot be made from 2s, so `-1`.

problems.approach: best[a] is the fewest coins for amount a. For each a try every coin c and take best[a - c] + 1 when it is smaller.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.statement: Return the length of the longest STRICTLY increasing subsequence of `nums` (items taken in order, not necessarily next to each other).
constraints: O(n log n) is possible and needed for the largest inputs

examples.explanation: `2, 3, 7, 101` has length 4.
Equal numbers do not count as increasing.

problems.approach: Keep tails[k], the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each number, binary search its place in tails and replace or append.

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.statement: Change `begin` into `end` one letter at a time. Every intermediate word must be in `words`, and `end` itself must be in `words` too. Return the number of words in the shortest sequence, counting both `begin` and `end`, or `0` if there is no such sequence. All words are lowercase and have the same length.
constraints: begin is not necessarily in words

examples.explanation: `hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog` has 5 words.
Without `cog` in the list, the answer is 0.

problems.approach: Breadth-first search on words: from each word try changing each letter to every other letter and move to words that are in the list and not yet seen. The first time you reach `end` is the shortest.

problems.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
problems.statement: `lists` is a list of lists, each already sorted ascending. Merge them into ONE sorted list that keeps duplicates. Some lists can be empty.
constraints: Sorting the concatenation works but a heap is the expected approach

examples.explanation: The three lists merge into `[1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6]`.
Empty input lists give `[]`.

problems.approach: Keep a min-heap with the current head of every list. Pop the smallest, add it to the answer and push the next item of the same list.
problems.reference_solution:
import heapq


def merge_k_lists(lists):
    heap = [(l[0], i, 0) for i, l in enumerate(lists) if l]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    out = []
    while heap:
        v, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(v)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return out

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.statement: Return the minimum number of single-character operations (insert, delete or replace a character) needed to turn the string `a` into the string `b`.

examples.explanation: `horse` to `ros` takes 3 operations.
Turning an empty string into `abc` needs 3 inserts.

problems.approach: dp[i][j] is the distance between the first i letters of a and the first j of b. Take the cheapest of delete, insert and replace (free when the letters match).

problems.title: Count N-Queens
problems.statement: Place `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard so that no two attack each other (no shared row, column or diagonal). Return the number of different valid placements.

examples.explanation: 4 queens have 2 solutions.
2 and 3 queens have none.

problems.approach: Place one queen per row with backtracking. Keep sets of used columns and both diagonals (row - col and row + col) so each check is O(1).

problems.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
problems.statement: `s` contains only `(` and `)`. Return the length of the longest CONTIGUOUS substring that is a valid, balanced set of parentheses.

examples.explanation: In `(()` the longest valid part is `()`, length 2.
In `)()())` it is `()()`, length 4.

problems.approach: Keep a stack of indexes with the index of the last unmatched position at the bottom. When a pair closes, the valid length is the distance to the new top of the stack.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.statement: For every window of `k` consecutive numbers of `nums`, moving from left to right, return the maximum of the window. The answer has `len(nums) - k + 1` values.
constraints: Scanning each window fully is too slow for the largest inputs

examples.explanation: The windows of 3 have maximums 3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7.
With `k = 1` the answer is the list itself.

problems.approach: Keep a deque of indexes whose values decrease. Drop smaller values from the back when a new number arrives and drop the front when it leaves the window; the front is the maximum.
